newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels set to restart war, say Mobutu must go.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels set to restart war, say Mobutu must go.

text.p: Zaire rebels said on Sunday they were restarting the war against the Kinshasa-based government after a three-day pause and demanded the resignation of President Mobutu Sese Seko.

Rebel leader Laurent Kabila would probably go to South Africa soon to spur negotiations on Mobutu's departure from power, Bizima Karaha, foreign affairs commissioner in the rebel alliance, told a news conference in Goma.
"He (Kabila) will go to boost the negotiations, probably to South Africa," Karaha said, adding it was a "possibility" Kabila could meet Mobutu face-to-face.

Rebels of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo/Zaire (AFDL) took Zaire's second city, Lubumbashi, last week and now control virtually half the vast country after less than six months of fighting.
Mobutu, who has ruled Zaire since 1965 but is now ailing with cancer, said on Saturday he would consider direct talks with Kabila as a compatriot, but would not accept demands from him.
The rebels fighting to oust Mobutu said they had declared a "pause" in military operations in order to give Mobutu time to consider resigning.
"There will never be a ceasefire before negotiations, never, never, never," Karaha said.
"The (appointment of a) new prime minister shows that Mobutu wants violence... Those who say meet violence with violence are right," Karaha said.

"We have decided that we will not give Mobutu any more chance... We want them (the regime) to go -- and after they have left we will consider a ceasefire because if Mobutu leaves it will be the end of the war," he said.
The collapse of the government army has given the rebels the upper hand at the negotiating table, enabling them to maintain their demand for the resignation of Mobutu, diplomats say.

The rebel radio on Sunday said that Alliance forces were now in control at Kasumbalesa, the main border point with Zambia, where ex-government forces had earlier claimed to have taken over on behalf of the Alliance.
Kabila was willing to meet Mobutu but would not make the mistake of getting sucked into protracted negotiations which could keep Mobutu in power, Karaha said.

Karaha returned on Saturday from South Africa, where he led an Alliance delegation in the first round of talks with Zaire government envoys, chaired by U.N. special envoy to the Great Lakes region Mohamed Sahnoun.
